Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette: Dr. Michael Jensen, a 50-year-old psychologist from the Midwest, had spent the first half of his career teaching trauma theory to graduate students before his own life was upended. The assault that would later anchor his symptomatology occurred in the early evening of a humid summer night in a downtown bar that had recently opened a second location. He had gone in to meet a client for a private consultation, unaware that the bar's loud music, cheap whiskey, and neon lights were already becoming part of his routine. It was the smell of alcohol that would haunt him long after that night, the sudden blare of sirens that would later echo in his mind whenever a distant ambulance passed, and a feeling of discomfort that seemed to surface whenever the air grew still or when he was in an unfamiliar space. That night, a masked stranger forced his hand to the back of his throat, and the scent of cheap liquor, the clatter of bottles, and the echoing sound of a distant siren fused into a single, unbearable memory. When Michael stepped into a conference room to give a lecture, the faint aroma of the coffee served in the break room, reminiscent of the alcohol scent, would instantly bring him to a state of emotional numbness. He would freeze, feeling as though the world had become a room where his senses were muted, as if he were dead inside. The memory of that night, however, was never accessible in a coherent narrative; it stayed locked behind a door he could not open. His mind would simply flash the raw intensity of pain and fear, yet no clear images or details could be put into words. This inability to recall the event fully, coupled with a persistent sense of being reduced to an object rather than a person, caused Michael to believe that he was no longer capable of being the competent psychologist he had once been. Michael's belief that he had lost his professional competence and his humanity has, in turn, amplified his sensitivity to the triggers that first set the cycle in motion. The moment he passes a bar, the smell of alcohol triggers not only his emotional numbness but also the conviction that he is no longer capable of facing the world, prompting him to avoid even casual conversation with clients who mention drinking. When he hears sirens, he anticipates danger, his thoughts racing to the possibility that he might be targeted again, and his perception of self as a dehumanized object fuels a sense that he is merely a target, not a person. In his office, he now keeps the blinds closed, the lights dimmed, and his schedule tightly packed so that he rarely has the chance to encounter discomforting situations. Each avoidance reinforces the sense that he is not in control of his own life. The way Michael's memories are fragmented also feeds back into his negative appraisals. Because he cannot piece together the event in narrative form, the raw emotional surge he experiences when a trigger surfaces becomes even more overwhelming. The lack of a coherent story makes it difficult for him to process the event in a way that would allow him to reappraise it as a past trauma rather than an ongoing threat. Consequently, he continues to feel dehumanized, as if he is an object that cannot escape the memory's pull. His emotional numbness, then, is not a sign of recovery but a symptom that his mind has turned the memory into an endless loop of unprocessed feeling. In the months that followed, Michael's avoidance behaviors began to interfere with his daily work. He started missing client appointments because the smell of their office's air freshener reminded him of the night's assault. When a colleague asked him to review a case file over a bottle of wine, he declined, insisting that the aroma was too reminiscent of the bar. The cumulative effect of these avoidances manifested in a decline in his professional standing, as clients began to express concern over his reluctance to engage in social aspects of therapy. His wife, sensing his growing withdrawal, suggested therapy for him, but Michael resisted, certain that confronting the past would only reinforce his belief that he was incapable of moving forward. The decision to seek help finally came after a brief, but intense, episode at the end of a Friday evening. While walking home, the blaring sirens of a passing ambulance cut through the quiet of the street. Michael felt his heart pound, his breathing shallow, and he found himself unable to breathe again as the smell of gasoline from a nearby truck washed over him. He could not remember the assault, but the sheer intensity of his emotional response told him that the cycle was still active. He realized that if he could not stop the spiraling effect of triggers and negative appraisals on his memory, his career, his marriage, and his sense of self would continue to deteriorate. Now, he hopes that a structured therapeutic process will help him reframe his negative appraisals, gain access to the blocked memory, and ultimately reduce the power of the triggers that keep him frozen in that moment.
